HEEWON STYLE — a KOREAN WEBTOON movie still PAINTED like a premium digital painting, the look of a dramatic manhwa cover. A 2:1 movie frame composed for a 2:1 letterbox crop (nothing important at the top or bottom edge). The shot the scene names (wide establishing, two-shot, close-up, over-the-shoulder) from a dramatic camera angle (low three-quarter, worm's-eye, high overhead or dutch), never a flat straight-on catalogue pose. Named characters' FACES are drawn exactly like the attached character sheet: the same confident ink linework drawn BOLD and THICK with real line weight — a heavy tapered black contour around the whole silhouette and the hair mass, medium lines for folds and features, fine lines only for lashes and loose strands and manhwa face design (eye shape, brows, nose, jaw, hairline and hair), recognisably those characters, in the clothes the scene gives them. EVERYTHING ELSE IS PAINTED: visible textured brushwork — loose digital-paint strokes and dry-brush, charcoal-like hatching that follow every fold of the silk and every plate of armour, the shadows built from layered strokes, the brightest ridges laid in with single confident strokes, a faint paper-and-canvas grain; at the edges of the garments the linework breaks into loose sketchy strokes. MYTHIC PAINTED FINISH: rich saturated jewel-tone colour, never a muddy grey-brown wash; splashed sumi-ink spatter and dry-brush flying-white streaks breaking out at the frame edges; ONE bold sweeping painted ribbon of the scene's accent colour (cloth, smoke, banner, mist or light) carving across the composition like a brushstroke of legend. NOT flat cel-shading, NOT smooth airbrushed gradients, NOT a clean vector look, NOT photoreal, NOT 3D. Symmetric one-point shot down the length of Hanyuan Hall at night, lit like a Chinese historical drama. ONE device: two inward-facing lines of officials in dark robes with tablets, receding toward the dais on a reflective black floor. On the dais the emperor sits in yellow before a tall painted screen. Behind the screen, lit from behind by one lamp so she reads through the silk, the consort Wu stands, her head turned toward the officials. Red lanterns and many practical flames spill gold onto the floor; incense haze; cool blue-green shadows between the columns. REFERENCE SHEET. TOP ROW, left to right: LEFT face = gaozong, SECOND face = wuzetian. Copy each face exactly; give each person the dress the scene names. SMALLER SECOND ROW, left to right: place board pl_daming_night (keep this exact architecture and ground). THE THIRD EMPEROR Colour #b8935a. WU ZETIAN — Look: Hair piled into a tall looped Tang chignon fixed with gold combs and flower pins, painted crescent brows, a red flower mark (huadian) between the brows, red lips. Dress: Tang court dress: a short jacket over a long skirt tied high under the bust, a long translucent silk shawl (pibo) over the shoulders and trailing on the floor; vermilion and deep red silk with gold-thread borders. Colour #e879a6. PLACE Chang’an (장안) — attached board /pl_daming_night.png; keep this exact architecture and ground. Tang palace of Chang'an, drawn from the Daming Palace (大明宮) site and reconstruction models: Hanyuan Hall's concave ensemble — an eleven-bay hall with a double-eaved hipped roof of dark grey tiles and curled owl-tail ridge ends (chiwei), red columns, white plaster walls, lattice windows, raised on three tiers of rammed-earth terraces faced in ochre-red plaster and edged with white stone balustrades; the Dragon Tail Way ramps folding up the terraces; forward on each side the Xiangluan and Qifeng que-towers (three stepped pavilions on tall battered grey-brick piers) joined to the hall by long roofed corridors; a vast paved square below, entered through the five-doored Danfeng Gate. Wide low Tang proportions, deep eaves on massive bracket sets. Tang palette is VERMILION and WHITE (red columns, white walls); roofs are black-grey tile trimmed with green-glazed ridge and eave tiles (a little yellow and blue tricolour glaze); balustrade posts painted red, blue and green. YELLOW belongs to the emperor's robe; gold is gilt-bronze fittings, lamp-trees and firelight on vermilion. Interiors: dark polished stone floors, rows of vermilion columns, gauze hangings, a raised dais with a painted screen behind the throne. Never the Forbidden City, never all-yellow glazed roofs, never the modern reconstruction or a city skyline. Mood: TANG RENDER: predominantly DARK and INTIMIDATING Chinese ink painting (shuimohua) — black and grey ink washes, wet-on-wet ink bleeding into rice paper, dry calligraphic brush for roofs, columns, smoke and robes, the vermilion and gold reduced to small accents in a world of ink; officials, guards and other Tang figures are ink figures too. The ONE exception is the Second Emperor himself: he keeps the house webtoon figure render in full colour (yellow robe, black futou, drawn face), a coloured man inside an ink empire. Staged like a Chinese historical drama (Legend of the Demon Cat, The Longest Day in Chang'an) but lit as full Heewon tenebrism: night or blue hour; ONE dominant hard key per shot — a backlight through open doors or lattice, or one lamp-tree — and 75% of the frame crushed black with no fill; colour contrast — gold-yellow flame highlights against cool blue-green in the few lit shadows; the other flames (lamp-trees, silk lanterns with no writing, braziers) are small points and round bokeh IN the black, never lighting the room evenly; red lantern light through lattice as one pattern on the floor; incense haze only inside the key shaft; polished dark floors reflecting the flames. Staged like a drama, at true human scale: camera at eye or knee height on a dolly or crane; court officials in two lines facing inward along the central aisle with tablets; banquet tables in two long facing rows with dancers in the centre and the emperor on the dais at the head; exteriors are real-scale terraces and corridors, the hall large but never a fantasy fortress. BACKGROUND AND LIGHT (painterly tenebrism): the background IS the place and the moment of the scene — open sky if they are in the sky, the hall if they are in a hall, the gate, the river, the snow — painted loosely in atmospheric brushwork (drifting smoke, cloud, haze, mist, falling snow, embers) in the scene's own colours, soft and out of focus, with a faint bokeh of small lights; it has colour, weather and depth — never a flat black void, never a detailed set; crowds and armies only as massed painted shapes dissolving into haze. ONE hard directional key light that belongs to the place (a brazier, a lamp, the sun through cloud, a torch, moonlight) rakes across the faces and clothes from the side or from below, modelling them in high contrast with deep painted shadows and a thin edge of the same light along the silhouette. Each character's colour lives in that light and in the atmosphere around them — never a glow aura or halo. Faces and bodies act the beat: real expressions, real weight, mid-motion. Faces from the sheet; new poses, never the sheet's stance. Each named person appears once, never cloned. Everyone wears period clothing of their own court (Korean, Tang, Yamato, Mohe furs), never European dress. No text, no speech bubbles, no panel borders, no watermark. NIGHT GROUND: the frame is built on BLACK — crushed ink-black night masses around the subject, the place pulled out of the dark only where the one key light (fire, lamp, torch, moon) falls, small warm bokeh in the black; the figure is the bright thing in a dark frame.
